newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine police given 'last chance' to reform.
newsitem.headline: Argentine police given 'last chance' to reform.

text.p: Argentina's biggest police force, which even top authorities say is so riddled with crime and corruption it inspires more fear than trust, was given an ultimatum on Friday to clean up its act.

The Buenos Aires Provincial Police, entrusted to protect the 13 million inhabitants of the province around the capital, was ordered by provincial Gov. Eduardo Duhalde to "reconcile itself with the society it is supposed to serve" or be given a civilian boss.

But Duhalde, also second-in-charge of the ruling Peronist Party, former vice-president and 1999 presidential hopeful, received a death threat for his decision to put all 48,000 agents on "dispensable" status, meaning they can be fired.

"The letter warns me they will make me "dispensable" and that I'll be looking at the radishes from under the earth," Duhalde, apparently unruffled, told reporters. "But anyone who wanted to kill me wouldn't write letters."

The Peronist governor summoned 1,000 top provincial police officers for a tough 20-minute dressing-down on Friday at which he repeated his threat to put a civilian in charge -- something experts have warned could cause huge resentment.

"I told them it could be their last chance to keep on trying to reform with a man from the force in charge," said Duhalde, expressing his "feeling of disdain for the rotten cops" and "traitors" who give the force a bad name.

The same size as the army and larger than the Federal Police, the Buenos Aires Provincial Police has such an image problem that when a news photographer was recently murdered in the province, policemen were among the first suspects.

The murder was a gruesome reminder of the paramilitary "death squads" of the 1970s. While the armed forces have put behind them the "Dirty War" nightmare of their 1976-83 regime, the Buenos Aires police remains tainted by brutality and fear.
So bad is its image that when Clarin newspaper carried the front-page headline "U.S. Says Buenos Aires Police Corrupt," many Argentines reacted by simply saying: "So what's new?"

Officers have been caught by television trafficking in drugs, four have been indicted for involvement in a 1994 bomb attack on a Jewish community centre that killed 86 people and there has been case after case of police brutality ranging from beatings to youngsters killed by trigger-happy officers.

Duhalde, shaken by the photographer's murder, acknowledges that "more and more people don't dare to file charges at a police station because they have lost trust. When people see a squad car at night, rather than feeling protected, they feel fear."
